claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is a uniform BCC phase at high temperature, for example at or above 1200 °C.
Phase stability in high-temperature BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by thermally activated partitioning among Cr, Co, Fe, Ni, and Al.
Under slow cooling or intermediate-to-low temperatures, thermodynamic driving forces and diffusion-limited kinetics promote B2 or other intermetallic formation from the BCC matrix.
Faster cooling suppresses solid-state phase transformations in the target alloy.
Local Al enrichment, potentially accompanied by ordering with Ni, increases the driving force for B2-like ordering and related intermetallic precipitation.
Diffusion of Al and Ni creates local compositional fluctuations that lower the free energy of ordered B2 relative to disordered BCC.
Intermediate-temperature holds or slow cooling provide sufficient time for intermetallic precipitates to nucleate and grow.
Rapid quenching suppresses precipitation because diffusion is kinetically limited.
Slower cooling or intermediate-temperature holds will produce more B2 or related intermetallic precipitation than rapid quenching.
B2 ordering will produce emerging superlattice reflections in XRD.
The transformed phase fraction will increase as cooling rate decreases or dwell time increases.
A rapid water quench from approximately 1200 °C retains disordered BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 with minimal transformation.
In situ high-temperature XRD can reveal temperature-dependent phase transformations, new phases, and transformation start and finish temperatures.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 between 600 and 1200 °C.
Composition changes larger than about ±1–2 at.% or substantially different thermal paths may alter precipitation pathways.
Composition changes or altered thermal paths may favor additional phases such as sigma or Laves.
Exact phase fractions and microstructures depend on cooling trajectory and minor compositional variation.

Failure to form B2 or another predicted intermetallic under slow cooling, or formation of a high intermetallic fraction after rapid quenching, would falsify the proposed thermodynamic–kinetic mechanism.
